question.prompt:
Two congruent circles centered at points \(A\) and \(B\) each pass through the other circle’s center. The line containing both \(A\) and \(B\) is extended to intersect the circles at points \(C\) and \(D.\)

The circles intersect at two points, one of which is \(E.\) What is the degree measure of \(\angle CED?\)

solutions.explanation:
The two new intersections of the extended line lie beyond the centers. Call the point beyond \(A\) point \(C\), and the point beyond \(B\) point \(D\), so their order is \(C,A,B,D\). Exchanging the names \(C\) and \(D\) does not change the requested angle.

Each circle passes through the other center, so their common radius equals \(AB\). Since \(E\) lies on both circles,
\[
AB=AE=BE.
\]
Thus triangle \(ABE\) is equilateral, and all its angles are \(60^\circ\).

Because \(AC\) and \(AB\) point in opposite directions,
\[
\angle CAE=180^\circ-60^\circ=120^\circ.
\]
Also, \(AC=AE\), since both are radii of the circle centered at \(A\). Triangle \(CAE\) is therefore isosceles, and its two equal base angles are
\[
\angle CEA=\frac{180^\circ-120^\circ}{2}=30^\circ.
\]
At the other center, \(BD\) and \(BA\) point in opposite directions, so \(\angle EBD=120^\circ\). Since \(BE=BD\), the same triangle-angle calculation gives \(\angle BED=30^\circ\).

The points \(A\) and \(B\) lie between \(C\) and \(D\), so the rays \(EA\) and \(EB\) divide \(\angle CED\) into these three adjacent angles. Hence
\[
\angle CED=30^\circ+60^\circ+30^\circ=\boxed{120^\circ},
\]
choice \(\text{C}\). The reasoning applies to either circle intersection chosen as \(E\).
solutions.title: Use triangles formed by radii
